# Volume 2 Chapter 9 The PlayStation

# Volume 2 Chapter 9 The PlayStation

Chapter 9
The PlayStation

## Part 1 Ohga's Decision: "Do it!"

The video game market throughout much of the 1980s was dominated by Nintendo's Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), and after news of Nintendo starting development on the next-generation Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) reached the ears of Sony, discussions arose concerning a potential technological collaboration between the two companies. Although Sony had not expanded into the video game market yet, the possibility of using the Sony-developed CD-ROM in place of the ROM cartridges used in the industry up until that point gave the two companies the chance to create a truly new type of gaming console.

Thus, a contract was finalized in early 1990 on the joint development of what would later be referred to as the Super NES CD-ROM, a fully integrated CD-ROM gaming console, between Sony and Nintendo. This proposed console was tentatively named the "PlayStation," though the collaboration ultimately never came to fruition. Image

From left, Sony Computer Entertainment President Tokunaka and then-Senior Managing Director Kutaragi holding the 18th Ibuka Award and 1996 Excellent Performance Award

## Part 3 Now Available: the PlayStation

In the winter of 1994, one year after SCE's founding, Sony's independently developed and long-awaited PlayStation video game console was finally born, created from the fusion of Sony's hardware and SMEJ's software expertise. Sporting high-resolution backgrounds and the ability to render multiple 3D-CG characters in real-time through a proprietary 32-bit CPU, the PlayStation was also capable of producing high quality sound which rivaled that of a music CD. Before development was fully off the ground, many people throughout the company were of the opinion that the device was simply a toy, sometimes explicitly questioning why Sony was working on children's toys all of a sudden. It was clear once the device was finished, however, that this was far beyond the level of a mere toy.

Featuring specs rivaling that of any high-end workstation of the day, the PlayStation was put to market on December 3 that same year at the shockingly low price of 39,800 yen, accompanied by a fresh and striking marketing campaign. Though the Sony brand name held little weight in the video game industry, the first one hundred thousand units sold in the blink of an eye, and the device soon went on to sell one million units within just half a year, becoming an era-defining hit in the world of video games.

The PlayStation's success could not entirely be chalked up to its beautiful graphics or vast library of titles, however. Utilizing CD-ROMs as its primary media format gave the device a significant edge when it came to distribution.

ROM cartridges, the standard form of video game media up until the PlayStation, took more time to produce than CD-ROMs, meaning it would take several months after stock was depleted before the product could be made available again. Since the PlayStation used CD-ROMs, for which SMEJ already possessed a strong production and distribution system, it took a maximum of six days - the same turnaround time as music CDs - for an order to be fulfilled, even when ordered in small lots. Production costs were minimal, especially when considering the vast amount of data required to support 3D-CG. SCE was also able to revolutionize distribution methods for video games, as instead of selling through wholesalers according to the industry norm, SCE established a distribution system which allowed game developers to sell their games directly to retailers. By enabling high-speed production and low costs, and with its improved distribution methods, the CD-ROM played a crucial role in the PlayStation's explosive success.

The device's advanced hardware design also caught the eyes of many. Featuring an exceptionally simple design - a round CD drive mounted on top of a rectangular body - the controller was also made with the user's hands in mind, sporting handles for users to grip. This controller shape was a striking departure from the standard flat controllers of the time. The symbols adorning the controller's buttons would go on to become a famous iconic aspect of the PlayStation in the future and were originally chosen by designer Teiyu Goto, who cited his desire to use "simple shapes that could easily be used as icons."

Receiving raving reviews across the globe, the PlayStation would achieve ten million units sold by the end of November 1996. Selling this many units in such a short amount of time was a record among all of Sony's products up until that point.

There have always been indie games – heck, they pre-date non-indie games! The tales of lone creators making games for the Apple, the Commodore 64, the Sinclair and many other 8-bit micros are legendary. These games would be “packaged” in ziplock bags with mimeographed instructions (sometimes!) and sold at the local computer shops. As the shift to a digitalized world continued to come into its own, Xbox Live Arcade (XBLA) made one of the first major steps to bringing these independent games to a major publishing platform in the waning days of the OG Xbox and ultimately taking off on Xbox 360.

The original founders of XBLA really saw it as an arcade – a place to play vintage arcade games and casual games on a core gamer system. A funny thing happened though. Some of those independent developers who were still making games on PC – folks like Jonathan Blow and the team at The Behemoth – saw those downloadable games and started to get some ideas. And pretty soon, with the encouragement and excitement of the folks at Microsoft at the time, new games, original games, games from independent developers started to appear on XBLA. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
